title: Suspected bacterial meningitis at 40 after kidney transplant, on vancomycin and ceftriaxone without ampicillin

provenance.author: Claude Code (draft for owner review), Listeria risk-factor rule (owner decision 2026-11-12)

clinical_review.notes: Owner approved the Listeria risk-factor cases as drafted (after the OpenEvidence review of the rule's evidence).

story: A 40-year-old woman who received a kidney transplant three years ago, on tacrolimus and mycophenolate, presents with fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and new confusion. Lumbar puncture shows a neutrophilic pleocytosis with low glucose and high protein. Empiric vancomycin, ceftriaxone 2 g every 12 hours and dexamethasone are started; CSF and blood cultures are pending. Ampicillin is not ordered.

problems.title: Long term use of calcineurin inhibitor (tacrolimus)

expected_findings.summary: Empiric therapy for suspected bacterial meningitis in a patient with a kidney transplant on immunosuppressive therapy lacks ampicillin: cephalosporins and vancomycin do not cover Listeria monocytogenes.

reference_answer: Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours (a full first dose, then intervals adjusted to graft function) to vancomycin, ceftriaxone and dexamethasone until cultures exclude Listeria; with a serious penicillin allergy, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the usual alternative. The ceftriaxone backbone is consistent with ESCMID 2016 and WHO 2025; some reviews prefer cefepime or meropenem in immunocompromised hosts, a clinician's choice that the rules do not flag. In a transplant recipient, also consider cryptococcal and tuberculous meningitis. Narrow therapy when cultures return.
rationale: Immunosuppressive therapy after transplantation is the strongest clinical discriminator of Listeria from pneumococcal meningitis, and Listeria is intrinsically resistant to cephalosporins. ESCMID 2016 adds amoxicillin or ampicillin for adults with Listeria risk factors at any age; the age rule alone would miss this 40-year-old. The finding rests on the transplant and immunosuppressant problems, the working diagnosis and the absence of an ampicillin order.

citations.supports: Empiric amoxicillin or ampicillin for Listeria, added to cefotaxime or ceftriaxone, in adults over 50 and in adults 18 to 50 with Listeria risk factors (Table 4.1 footnote: diabetes mellitus, immunosuppressive drugs, cancer, other immunocompromising conditions).

Add ampicillin or amoxicillin to the initial empiric regimen with any Listeria risk factor, including organ transplantation and immunosuppressive therapy; checked against the WHO document, 2026-11-12.
